Current commercial production uses fats, oils, and greases (FOG), as well as waste. Other anticipated feedstocks include the organic fraction of municipal solid waste (MSW), woody biomass, alcohol, and other biogenic resources. ASTM International is a voluntary consensus standards organization who creates, maintains, and updates jet fuel quality specifications and test methods. ASTM D7566, Standard Specification for Aviation Turbine Fuel Containing Synthesized Hydrocarbons, dictates fuel quality standards for non-petroleum-based jet fuel and outlines approved SAF-based fuel production pathways and the percentage allowable in a blend with Jet A.6 Currently, there are eight approved pathways in ASTM D7566 (Table 4). ASTM D1655, Standard Specification for Aviation Turbine Fuels, allows coprocessing of non-petroleum feedstocks at petroleum refineries at a rate of up to 5% and up to 10% for the biointermediates hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA). SAF must be blended with conventional jet fuel (from 10% to 50% depending on the annex, shown in Table 4). Existing commercial SAF plants all use the HEFA pathway, which is very similar to the technology used at petroleum refineries. In addition to SAF, HEFA plants produce renewable diesel and other renewable fuels and chemicals. Alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) commercial facilities are expected to be the next commercialized pathway.
